items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: I didn't know anything about Jimmie Lunceford, but Charlie Johnson wanted to hire Willie the first night he heard him.

ctx.x: He was getting a leader's fee of 65 dollars a week and taking 9 times 5 dollars a week from us, which made him have a 115 dollars a week. That really broke my heart, to think that we had such a promising future, and because of Cecil's greediness, it all went down the drain.

Sy Oliver, whom I had met not long after I had joined the Scott band and who was still quite young when we played his home town of Zanesville, Ohio, heard us at the Savoy one time (that was before he came to New York with Jimmie Lunceford) and told me that we did not have the best brass section in the business, but that we had the best YOUNG brass section he had ever heard.

Dickie, Frank, and I knew each other's feeling so well that if anyone of us wanted to play a riff behind a sax solo, which we often did, one would start a riff and the other would pick it up and get the feeling of it before one measure had passed, and we played them in harmony and not unison. And a riff was never exactly the same every time although the number was played often.

items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: Then Jimmy Lunceford came to town. His first trumpet player was named [Tommy] Stevenson, and he was the really first high note man I ever heard.

ctx.x: So Cecil lost the chance of being nationally known because he wanted to make big money but sacrificed the opportunity because he had stolen 45 dollars a week from us for Lord knows how many weeks and he did not want to stop the operation. Both Scott brothers were finished as orchestra leaders.

Even when I was gigging around with Cecil Scott, I was managing to get in quite a lot of practice. Mostly I was concerned to develop a stronger lip, to be able to play a long phrase, or sometimes to see how long I could hold one note. Range was important, but I never tried to be an altissimo trumpeter. Today I can make 'A' or even 'B' flat, above high 'C', though I cannot stay there. Even then, I could easily make 'F'. Trumpet players started to be able to do that after Louis recorded "I Can't Give You Anything…

In addition to playing scales or a phrase that I had never played before, I'd listen a lot to other people. I not only copied Louis Armstrong records, I also copied from pianists in order to try to see what they were doing. Even if you never use the same phrase, it's good to know it. People say that I play a lot of phrases with a lot of notes in them. I don't think the influence for that came from saxophone players. I was impressed by players like Jabbo Smith and Rex Stewart.
